patient.name: Kwame Asante
patient.complaint: Severe back and thigh pain for 2 days
background: Sickle cell disease (HbSS), diagnosed on newborn screening
Takes folic acid and penicillin V; vaccinations up to date
Student in Lewisham; parents from Ghana, both sickle trait

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with ethnicity plus an FBC: Cypriot with MCV 65 and near-normal Hb (beta-thal trait), Southeast Asian with normal ferritin (alpha-thal trait), or sickle cell with chest pain (acute chest syndrome).

points: Kwame, 19, **sickle cell disease (HbSS)** since newborn screening.
Two days of severe aching in his **lower back and both thighs**.
Started after a cold weekend at a festival, drinking little water.
Usual codeine at home has not touched it; pain **9/10**.

steps.lead: Kwame's sickle cell disease is one of the **haemoglobinopathies**: an inherited fault in haemoglobin, here its **structure** (HbS).
Kwame's parents are both from Ghana and both carry sickle trait: **African ancestry plus family history** are the key risk factors.

points: Tender lumbar spine and thighs, no swelling or redness.
Chest clear; spleen not palpable (auto-infarcted years ago).

steps.lead: Kwame shows the general picture: **anaemia, jaundice and pain**. Sickle cell gives pain; **bone deformity** points instead to thalassaemia major.

steps.title: Telling the haemoglobinopathies apart
head: Condition
Who
Key blood picture
Clue
rows: MCV very low, Hb near normal

steps.lead: Kwame's anaemia is not microcytic, so this is not thalassaemia. Learn these patterns: the exam loves a **Cypriot with MCV 65**.
Kwame's rigid **sickled cells** block small vessels in bone: a vaso-occlusive crisis. G6PD gives episodic haemolysis after a trigger, not bone pain.

steps.q: On day 2 Kwame develops **chest pain and breathlessness**, SpO2 91%. What must you suspect?
steps.r: Chest pain plus breathlessness in sickle cell is **acute chest syndrome** until proven otherwise: a medical emergency.

visual.title: Kwame's chest X-ray, day 2
visual.caption: New right lower zone infiltrate with chest pain, hypoxia and fever: acute chest syndrome.

steps.lead: Kwame now has **acute chest syndrome**; stroke and splenic dysfunction are the other big sickle complications. Thalassaemia's complications come from **transfusion iron**.

steps.text: Do not label new chest pain in sickle cell as 'more crisis pain'. Check SpO2 and get a **chest X-ray**: acute chest syndrome kills.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?' (haemoglobin electrophoresis) or 'most likely finding' (HbA2 >3.5%, haemolytic FBC).

steps.title: Kwame's bloods on arrival
steps.text: Low Hb, normal MCV, high reticulocytes, bilirubin and LDH: a haemolytic picture.

steps.lead: Kwame's FBC is the first-line test: a **haemolytic anaemia**. A thalassaemia would instead give a **microcytic** picture.

visual.title: MCV: where does the patient sit?
visual.label: Kwame 88
visual.caption: Sickle cell: normocytic. Thal trait: MCV around 65 with a near-normal Hb.

steps.q: Kwame's new GP wants written confirmation of his diagnosis. Which test is the gold standard?
steps.r: **Haemoglobin electrophoresis** separates HbS, HbA, HbA2 and HbF. A film suggests; electrophoresis confirms.

steps.lead: Kwame's electrophoresis shows **HbS with no HbA**. In thalassaemia it shows raised **HbF or HbA2** instead.

steps.title: What electrophoresis shows
head: Condition
Electrophoresis
rows: HbS, **no HbA**, HbF a little raised

visual.title: HbA2 on electrophoresis
visual.label: Kwame's cousin 5.2%
visual.caption: Kwame's cousin (Cypriot father) has MCV 64: HbA2 above 3.5% confirms beta-thalassaemia trait.

steps.text: Microcytosis with a **normal ferritin** is thalassaemia until proven otherwise: the next test is **haemoglobin electrophoresis**.
A normal electrophoresis does **not** exclude alpha-thalassaemia trait: it looks normal. Clue: Southeast Asian, microcytic, normal ferritin.

management.exam: Expect acute sickle crisis (oxygen, IV fluids, analgesia), long-term hydroxyurea, transfusion for thal major and desferrioxamine for iron overload.

points: Kwame is curled up in pain, 9/10, and looks dry.
Last crisis admission was 2 months ago; four this year.

steps.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management of Kwame's crisis?
steps.r: Acute crisis = **oxygen, IV fluids and strong analgesia** (opioid, within 30 minutes). Hydroxyurea is long-term prevention.

steps.lead: Kwame gets **oxygen, IV fluids and IV morphine**. Thalassaemia's first-line is different: **transfusion**, lifelong and fortnightly in beta-thal major.

steps.title: Acute sickle crisis in ED
nodes: Look for infection: cultures, antibiotics if febrile
Chest pain or SpO2 falling: CXR for acute chest syndrome
Acute chest syndrome: senior and haematology input (exchange transfusion)
steps.caption: Treat the pain fast, then hunt for the complications.

visual.title: Kwame's pain score
visual.caption: Rapid opioid analgesia, fluids and oxygen bring the pain down; he goes home on day 4.

steps.lead: Four crises a year: Kwame starts **hydroxyurea**, and stays on **penicillin prophylaxis** and **vaccines** because his spleen does not work.

steps.text: Repeated transfusion means **iron overload**: the answer is **desferrioxamine** chelation, never venesection in an anaemic patient.
Thalassaemia **trait** needs no treatment, and **oral iron is wrong** when ferritin is normal. Counsel about partner testing instead.

science.exam: Expect mechanism questions: HbS polymerisation on deoxygenation, how hydroxyurea works (HbF), why G6PD deficiency haemolyses, and autosomal recessive inheritance.

steps.title: Why Kwame's bones hurt
nodes: Small vessels blocked: ischaemic bone pain

steps.lead: Cold and dehydration lowered Kwame's oxygen and raised blood viscosity, so his **HbS polymerised** and sickled cells blocked marrow vessels.

steps.r: Hydroxyurea raises **HbF**, which does not join HbS polymers, so fewer cells sickle.

steps.lead: Kwame's hydroxyurea works by boosting **HbF**, which dilutes HbS and interferes with polymerisation.
Unlike Kwame, a child with beta-thal major has **unpaired chains** that destroy red cell precursors, so the marrow expands: **frontal bossing**.
If Kwame ever needs regular transfusions, each unit adds iron he cannot excrete, so he would need **desferrioxamine**.
G6PD is a different red cell problem: without **NADPH**, glutathione cannot neutralise oxidants, so a trigger drug causes haemolysis.

steps.text: Inheritance: sickle cell and thalassaemia are **autosomal recessive**. Two carrier parents: **1 in 4** chance of an affected child each pregnancy.

mcq.q: What is the usual mode of inheritance of haemoglobinopathies?
mcq.r: Sickle cell and thalassaemia are **autosomal recessive**; G6PD deficiency is the X-linked exception.

mcq.q: Which group has the highest risk of thalassaemia?
mcq.r: Thalassaemia is commonest in **Mediterranean and Far Eastern** families.

mcq.q: Which HbA2 level supports beta-thalassaemia trait?
Which haemoglobin forms in alpha-thalassaemia major?
mcq.r: All 4 alpha genes deleted: **HbBart's**, causing hydrops fetalis, incompatible with life.

mcq.q: A sickle cell patient has chest pain and breathlessness. What do you suspect?
mcq.r: **Acute chest syndrome** is the emergency to exclude.

mcq.q: Which blood film finding is classic for G6PD deficiency?
What is the gold standard investigation for haemoglobinopathies?
mcq.r: **Haemoglobin electrophoresis** identifies and quantifies each Hb type.

mcq.q: How often does beta-thalassaemia major need transfusion?
Which drug treats transfusional iron overload?
Why do red cells sickle in HbSS?
mcq.r: Deoxygenated **HbS polymerises**, making cells rigid and sickle-shaped.

glossary.Haemoglobinopathies: Inherited disorders of haemoglobin structure (e.g. sickle cell) or synthesis (thalassaemia).
glossary.HbS: Sickle haemoglobin, from a point mutation in beta-globin; it polymerises when deoxygenated.
glossary.HbSS: Two copies of the sickle gene: sickle cell disease.
glossary.HbA: Normal adult haemoglobin: two alpha and two beta chains.
glossary.HbA2: Minor adult haemoglobin (two alpha, two delta chains); above 3.5% suggests beta-thalassaemia trait.
glossary.HbF: Fetal haemoglobin (two alpha, two gamma chains); it does not sickle.
glossary.HbBart's: Haemoglobin made of four gamma chains, seen when all four alpha genes are deleted.
glossary.Bart's hydrops fetalis: Alpha-thalassaemia major: severe fetal anaemia and oedema, incompatible with life.
glossary.Thalassaemia: Reduced or absent synthesis of alpha or beta globin chains, giving microcytic anaemia.
glossary.Beta-thalassaemia trait: Carrier state for beta-thalassaemia: often no symptoms, very low MCV, HbA2 above 3.5%.
glossary.Beta-thalassaemia major: Both beta genes faulty: severe anaemia in infancy needing lifelong transfusion.
glossary.Alpha-thalassaemia trait: Carrier state for alpha-thalassaemia: mild microcytosis, normal ferritin and normal electrophoresis.
glossary.Sickle cell disease: Inherited disorder where HbS makes red cells rigid and sickle-shaped, causing haemolysis and vaso-occlusion.
glossary.Vaso-occlusive crisis: Painful episode where sickled cells block small vessels, causing ischaemia, often in bone.
glossary.Acute chest syndrome: Sickle cell emergency: chest pain, breathlessness, hypoxia and a new infiltrate on chest X-ray.
glossary.G6PD deficiency: X-linked enzyme deficiency leaving red cells unable to resist oxidative stress, so triggers cause haemolysis.
glossary.Bite cells: Red cells with a 'bite' removed where the spleen took out denatured haemoglobin; classic of G6PD deficiency.
glossary.Basophilic stippling: Blue dots in red cells from leftover ribosomal RNA; seen in thalassaemia and lead poisoning.
glossary.Reticulocytosis: Raised immature red cells in the blood, showing the marrow is replacing destroyed cells.
glossary.Polychromasia: Bluish-tinged young red cells on a film, reflecting high reticulocyte output.
glossary.Microcytic: Red cells smaller than normal (MCV below 80 fL).
glossary.MCV: Mean cell volume: the average red cell size.
glossary.Haemoglobin electrophoresis: Test that separates and measures each haemoglobin type; gold standard for haemoglobinopathies.
glossary.Frontal bossing: Prominent forehead from marrow expansion in the skull bones.
glossary.Hepatosplenomegaly: Enlargement of both liver and spleen.
glossary.Haemosiderosis: Iron deposition in tissues, here from repeated transfusions.
glossary.Iron chelation: Drug treatment that binds excess iron so it can be excreted.
glossary.Desferrioxamine: Iron chelator given to treat or prevent transfusional iron overload.
glossary.Hydroxyurea: Oral drug that raises HbF and reduces sickle crises (also called hydroxycarbamide).
glossary.Ineffective erythropoiesis: Red cell precursors die in the marrow before they mature.
glossary.NADPH: Reducing molecule made by the pentose phosphate pathway; keeps glutathione active.
glossary.Glutathione: Antioxidant that protects red cells from oxidative damage.
glossary.Primaquine: Antimalarial drug that can trigger haemolysis in G6PD deficiency.
glossary.Hyposplenism: Poor splenic function, raising the risk of infection by encapsulated bacteria.
glossary.Haemolytic anaemia: Anaemia from early red cell destruction: raised reticulocytes, bilirubin and LDH.
glossary.LDH: Lactate dehydrogenase: an enzyme released from destroyed cells, raised in haemolysis.
glossary.Autosomal recessive: Inheritance needing two faulty copies; carriers usually have no or mild disease.

technique.stem: A 23 year old woman of Cypriot descent has a routine blood test before starting a new job. She feels well and has no symptoms. Her periods are regular and not heavy. Examination is normal.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: Diagnosis from a blood test: compare the MCV with the Hb.
Mediterranean ancestry, no symptoms, no blood loss; the labs show **MCV very low for a near-normal Hb** and normal ferritin.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Disproportionate microcytosis in a well Cypriot: **beta-thalassaemia trait**.

elim: No chronic illness, and it is usually normocytic with a raised ferritin.
Major presents in infancy with severe anaemia; she is well with a near-normal Hb.
Ferritin is normal and periods are not heavy; MCV falls in proportion to Hb.
Causes a macrocytic, not microcytic, anaemia.

steps.x: **C. Beta-thalassaemia trait.** Rule: MCV in the 60s with Hb nearly normal and normal ferritin = thal trait; confirm with HbA2 >3.5%.

technique.stem: A 29 year old man of Greek descent is found to have a haemoglobin of 131 g/L and an MCV of 63 fL on a routine blood test. His ferritin is normal. He has no symptoms. Haemoglobin electrophoresis is requested.
technique.q: Which is the most likely finding on haemoglobin electrophoresis?

steps.x: A 'most likely finding' question: decide the diagnosis, then its result.
Mediterranean, near-normal Hb, very low MCV, normal ferritin, well.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Beta-thalassaemia trait, so **HbA2 above 3.5%**.

elim: Absent HbA is beta-thal major, a severe illness of infancy.
HbBart's means all four alpha genes are deleted: fatal in utero.
HbS is sickle cell; it gives a normocytic haemolytic picture.
A normal pattern fits alpha-thal trait, typically Southeast Asian.

steps.x: **E. Raised HbA2.** Rule: beta-thal trait = HbA2 >3.5%; alpha-thal trait = normal electrophoresis.

technique.stem: A 14 month old boy of Italian descent has pallor, poor feeding and a swollen abdomen. He has hepatosplenomegaly. Haemoglobin electrophoresis shows no HbA with raised HbF and HbA2. His haemoglobin is 58 g/L.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate long-term management?

steps.x: Long-term management of a confirmed diagnosis.

clues: no HbA with raised HbF and HbA2
steps.x: Infant, Mediterranean, HSM, no HbA: **beta-thalassaemia major**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Lifelong **fortnightly blood transfusions**, plus iron chelation later.

elim: Hydroxyurea is for sickle cell disease.
He is not iron deficient; iron would worsen overload.
Hb 58 g/L in an infant is life-threatening anaemia.
Splenectomy is not first-line and does not replace transfusion.

steps.x: **D. Regular blood transfusions.** Rule: beta-thal major = transfusion for life plus desferrioxamine for the iron.

technique.stem: A 17 year old boy with sickle cell disease has severe pain in his legs after swimming in a cold lake. His temperature is 37.2°C and oxygen saturation 94% breathing air.
technique.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his pain?

steps.x: Mechanism question: name the step that causes the pain.
Cold and low oxygen are classic sickling triggers.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Deoxygenated **HbS polymerises**, cells sickle and block small vessels.

elim: Sickle cell is not autoimmune.
That is beta-thalassaemia.
Iron overload is chronic, from transfusions.
That is G6PD deficiency.

steps.x: **E. Polymerisation of deoxygenated HbS.** Rule: HbS polymerises when deoxygenated, causing vaso-occlusion.

practice.stem: A 21 year old man with sickle cell disease has had pain in his back and legs for 2 days. Today he has developed right-sided chest pain and breathlessness. His temperature is 38.1°C, pulse rate 118 bpm, BP 122/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 90% breathing air. A chest X-ray is performed (see item resources).
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Chest pain, breathlessness, hypoxia, fever and a new infiltrate in sickle cell disease define acute chest syndrome. Pneumonia alone is the main thing it mimics; treat it as an emergency.

steps.x: Diagnosis in a known sickle cell patient: think complications.
Chest pain, breathlessness, fever and hypoxia with a new infiltrate.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Acute chest syndrome**.

elim: Does not explain hypoxia, fever or a new infiltrate.
Shows a lung edge, not consolidation, and is not typical in sickle cell.
No cardiac history; it gives bilateral changes.
Causes a big spleen and falling Hb, not chest signs.

steps.x: **A. Acute chest syndrome.** Rule: chest pain + breathlessness in sickle cell = acute chest syndrome, an emergency.

practice.stem: A 10 month old girl of Greek descent is brought to the GP because she is pale, feeding poorly and not gaining weight. Her forehead is prominent and her abdomen is full, with a liver edge and spleen both palpable. Her pulse rate is 168 bpm and respiratory rate 40 breaths per minute.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Beta-thalassaemia major presents in the first year of life with severe anaemia, failure to thrive, hepatosplenomegaly and frontal bossing from marrow expansion. Traits are mild.

steps.x: Diagnosis in an infant with anaemia.

clues: liver edge and spleen both palpable
steps.x: First year of life, Mediterranean, failure to thrive, frontal bossing, hepatosplenomegaly, tachycardia.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Beta-thalassaemia major**.

elim: Trait is mild and usually found incidentally.
Trait is usually asymptomatic with near-normal Hb.
Causes haemolysis and splenomegaly but not frontal bossing; not Mediterranean-linked.
Would not give frontal bossing and hepatosplenomegaly.

steps.x: **B. Beta-thalassaemia major.** Rule: infant + bossing + HSM + Mediterranean = beta-thal major.

practice.stem: A 24 year old man of Sardinian descent has dark urine and yellow eyes 2 days after eating a meal containing fava beans. He is otherwise well.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Oxidative haemolysis after fava beans in a Mediterranean man is G6PD deficiency. Gilbert's raises bilirubin without anaemia.

steps.x: Diagnosis of an acute haemolysis.
Mediterranean man, fava bean trigger, haemolysis (low Hb, high reticulocytes and bilirubin).

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **G6PD deficiency**.

elim: Not food-triggered; DAT would be positive.
Trait does not cause acute haemolysis.
Causes jaundice without anaemia or dark urine.
No trigger link; spherocytes on the film.

steps.x: **C. G6PD deficiency.** Rule: haemolysis after fava beans or an oxidant drug = G6PD deficiency; look for bite cells.

practice.stem: A 32 year old woman originally from Vietnam has a blood test at her antenatal booking visit. She feels well. The blood film shows microcytic cells with basophilic stippling. Haemoglobin electrophoresis is normal.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Alpha-thalassaemia trait gives microcytosis with normal ferritin and normal electrophoresis. Beta-thal trait would raise HbA2.

steps.x: Diagnosis from bloods: microcytosis with a normal ferritin.
Southeast Asian, mild microcytic anaemia, normal ferritin, stippling, **normal** electrophoresis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Alpha-thalassaemia trait**.

elim: No chronic illness; ferritin would be raised.
Electrophoresis would show HbA2 >3.5%.
Ferritin is normal.
Rare; needs ring sideroblasts in the marrow and iron is high.

steps.x: **A. Alpha-thalassaemia trait.** Rule: microcytic + normal ferritin + normal electrophoresis + Southeast Asian = alpha-thal trait.

practice.stem: A 27 year old man with beta-thalassaemia major has had fortnightly blood transfusions since infancy. He often misses his iron chelation. He has painful knuckles and his skin has darkened. His pulse rate is 86 bpm and BP 118/72 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
practice.e: Each transfusion adds iron the body cannot excrete. Missed chelation leads to iron overload with MCP arthropathy and pigmentation.

steps.x: Asking for a cause: link the symptoms to his treatment.
Years of transfusion, poor chelation, MCP joint pain, hyperpigmented skin.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Transfusional iron overload** (haemosiderosis).

elim: Would give low BP and hyponatraemia; the transfusion history explains this.
Affects the big toe, not the MCP joints with skin darkening.
His iron comes from transfusions, not a HFE mutation.
Does not darken the skin; he has a clear iron source.

steps.x: **E. Transfusional iron overload.** Rule: transfused thal patient + MCP joints + bronze skin = iron overload; give desferrioxamine.

practice.stem: A 7 year old boy with sickle cell disease suddenly develops weakness of his left arm and the left side of his face, with slurred speech. His temperature is 36.9°C, pulse rate 96 bpm and BP 108/66 mmHg. Capillary glucose is 5.2 mmol/L.
practice.q: Which is the most likely complication?
practice.e: Stroke is a classic sickle cell complication, even in children. Normal glucose and no fever make the distractors unlikely.

steps.x: Complication of sickle cell disease.

clues: left arm and the left side of his face
steps.x: Sudden focal neurology in a child with sickle cell disease.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Ischaemic stroke** from sickling in cerebral vessels.

elim: No chest symptoms.
Bell's affects only the face; his arm is weak.
Glucose is normal.
No fever or neck stiffness.

steps.x: **D. Ischaemic stroke.** Rule: sudden weakness in a sickle child = stroke; call haematology for urgent exchange transfusion.

practice.stem: A 27 year old woman of Turkish Cypriot descent attends antenatal booking. She is well and has no heavy periods. Her partner is of Greek descent.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
practice.e: Haemoglobin electrophoresis is gold standard for haemoglobinopathies and shows raised HbA2 in beta-thal trait. Partner testing follows.

steps.x: Diagnostic test for suspected thalassaemia.
Mediterranean woman, microcytosis with near-normal Hb and normal ferritin.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Haemoglobin electrophoresis**, the gold standard.

elim: Suggestive, not diagnostic.

B12 deficiency is macrocytic.

practice.stem: A 20 year old man with sickle cell disease attends clinic feeling more tired than usual. He is mildly jaundiced. His pulse rate is 92 bpm and BP 116/70 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on full blood count and reticulocyte count?
practice.e: Sickle cell disease causes chronic haemolytic anaemia, so the marrow responds with reticulocytosis. Microcytosis belongs to thalassaemia and iron deficiency.

steps.x: Most likely finding on a first-line test.
Sickle cell disease means chronic haemolysis; jaundice confirms it.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Haemolytic** picture: normocytic anaemia, raised reticulocytes.

elim: That suggests B12 or folate deficiency.
That is iron deficiency.
Sickle cell disease causes chronic anaemia.
That is acute leukaemia.

steps.x: **D. Normocytic anaemia with raised reticulocytes.** Rule: sickle = haemolytic FBC; thalassaemia = microcytic FBC.

practice.stem: A 22 year old woman with sickle cell disease presents to the emergency department with severe pain in her arms and chest wall after a long flight. Her temperature is 37.4°C, pulse rate 112 bpm, BP 124/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 93% breathing air. Chest X-ray is clear.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
practice.e: Acute sickle crisis is treated with oxygen, IV fluids and analgesia. Hydroxyurea prevents crises but does not treat one.

steps.x: Initial management of an acute crisis.
Vaso-occlusive crisis after dehydration and hypoxia on a flight; CXR clear so no acute chest syndrome yet.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Oxygen, IV fluids and analgesia**.

elim: Long-term prevention, not acute treatment.
For iron overload, not a crisis.
Undertreats severe pain and hypoxia.
Not a crisis treatment.

steps.x: **D. Oxygen, IV fluids and analgesia.** Rule: acute sickle crisis = oxygen, fluids, strong analgesia within 30 minutes.

practice.stem: A 23 year old man with sickle cell disease has had five admissions with painful crises in the past year. He takes folic acid and penicillin V and his vaccinations are up to date.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate long-term management?
practice.e: Hydroxyurea raises HbF and reduces vaso-occlusive crises. Antibiotics and vaccines are already in place.

steps.x: Long-term management to prevent crises.
Frequent crises despite standard prophylaxis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Hydroxyurea**.

elim: For iron overload, not crisis prevention.
A tyrosine kinase inhibitor for CML.
He is not iron deficient.
His spleen is already non-functional; it does not prevent crises.

steps.x: **B. Hydroxyurea.** Rule: recurrent sickle crises = hydroxyurea.

practice.stem: A 16 year old girl with beta-thalassaemia major receives transfusions every 2 weeks. She is well. Her pulse rate is 80 bpm and BP 110/68 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate additional treatment?
practice.e: Repeated transfusions deliver iron faster than it can be excreted; desferrioxamine chelates it. Venesection is for hereditary haemochromatosis, not anaemic patients.

steps.x: Additional treatment for a complication of treatment.
Lifelong transfusions with a ferritin far above range.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Desferrioxamine** iron chelation.

elim: Used in sickle cell disease.
Would worsen iron overload.
Does not treat iron overload.
Removes blood she needs; she is transfusion-dependent.

steps.x: **A. Desferrioxamine.** Rule: transfusional iron overload = chelation, never venesection.

practice.stem: A 25 year old woman with sickle cell disease starts hydroxyurea after repeated painful crises. Over the next year her crises become much less frequent.
practice.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of this benefit?
o: Correction of the beta-globin point mutation
